extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for choosing words and phrasing in academic argument papers to maximize clarity, concision, and appropriate register, including strategies for thesis wording and use of key terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall goal: word-level clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Revise papers for word-level clarity, eliminate wordiness and avoid clichés, find the words that best express your ideas, and choose words that suit an academic audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As you revise, ask “Is this really what I mean?” and “Will readers understand this?” Be willing to rewrite sentences from scratch to choose words with greater clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixing awkward, vague, or unclear sentences (reader perspective & syntax)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentences marked 'awkward,' 'vague,' or 'unclear' may be hard to follow because of grammatical problems or syntax, not just word choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read from a reader's point of view to see where a sentence changes direction or omits information. Identify misplaced modifiers or other structural issues (example: dangling modifier 'Having finished with studying, the pizza was quickly eaten' → revise to include the correct subject).

rubrics_metrics.name: Misused words
rubrics_metrics.description: The word doesn’t actually mean what the writer thinks it does.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether the word conveys the intended meaning; replace with a correct word (example: 'monotonous culture' → 'homogenous culture').

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid words with unwanted connotations
rubrics_metrics.description: Some word choices carry unintended meanings or connotations that distort what you mean.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose alternative words that remove unintended connotations (example: 'private places' for ants → 'hiding places').

rubrics_metrics.name: Pronoun clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Using a pronoun when readers can’t tell whom/what it refers to causes confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make antecedents explicit when needed (example: replace ambiguous 'he' with 'Jake' or reorder sentence so the referent is clear).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary jargon and technical terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Jargon or technical terms can make readers work unnecessarily hard; use them only when necessary for the field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the term is necessary, define or contextualize it; otherwise replace with simpler language (example: 'dialectical interface between neo-Platonists and anti-disestablishment Catholics' → 'dialogue between neo-Platonists and certain Catholic thinkers').

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid loaded language; define terms you rely on
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers sometimes rely on loaded words without spelling out what they mean, repeating them without clarifying the referent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spell out the specific phenomena or sources you mean rather than relying on broad loaded terms (example: 'society' → 'contemporary American popular media, like magazines and movies').

rubrics_metrics.name: Eliminate wordiness; prefer concise alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Wordy constructions use multiple words where fewer will do and reduce clarity/efficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for common multi-word phrases and replace them with shorter substitutes (examples: 'I came to the realization that' → 'I realized that'; 'In the event that' → 'If').

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid clichés
rubrics_metrics.description: Clichés are overused phrases that have become trite and often longer than necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize clichés and create shorter, fresher alternatives—prefer a single precise word when possible (examples: 'Dead as a doornail' → 'Dead'; 'Agree to disagree' → 'Disagree').

rubrics_metrics.name: Write for an academic audience: aim for simple clarity with appropriate formality
rubrics_metrics.description: Academic writing should communicate arguments clearly and convincingly rather than 'sound smart.' Use simple words; avoid slang and overly casual phrasing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simplicity does not equal simplicity of thought; avoid unfamiliar constructions intended only to impress. Maintain formality (avoid instant-message/colloquial tone) while prioritizing clear expression of thesis and argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting and using key terms: repetition vs. redundancy
rubrics_metrics.description: Repetition of key terms can be productive for cohesion and emphasis, while redundancy is tired, unnecessary repetition that signals lack of clarity or fatigue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberately repeat crucial terms in topic sentences and thesis for cohesion; revise when repetition is lazy or redundant. Use strategies (below) to revise redundancy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build clear thesis statements using precise key terms
rubrics_metrics.description: A strong thesis captures important elements and the significance of the argument using concise, appropriate key terms rather than vague qualifiers like 'important' or 'interesting.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine key terms to show how the argument will be made and why it matters. Revise multiple versions (example: compare three thesis drafts for specificity and argument strength).

rubrics_metrics.name: Be careful using unfamiliar words (check context and dictionary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Words you are unfamiliar with may have uses or connotations you don’t expect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine how a word is used in context and consult a dictionary to ensure it fits your intended meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the thesaurus cautiously; verify synonyms’ connotations
rubrics_metrics.description: Thesaurus suggestions may have different shades of meaning that don't fit your intended sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult a dictionary for each candidate synonym to confirm it matches the nuance you need.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid trying to impress with pompous diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex or inflated phrasing intended to 'sound smart' often reduces clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer the clearer, more direct phrasing—even if shorter or simpler—over convoluted alternatives (example contrasts provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize strong nouns and verbs before refining adjectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Accurate and specific nouns and verbs strengthen a sentence more than focusing first on adjectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revise 'book' and 'tells' into more informative nouns/verbs ('novel describes') before changing adjectives like 'good.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Slash/option technique for word choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Write out multiple choices for a questionable word or phrase inline (e.g., 'questionable/inaccurate/vague/inappropriate') and pick the best.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brainstorm several alternatives when stuck; select or combine terms to convey the precise meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Look for repetition and evaluate whether it is purposeful
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify repeated nouns, verbs, or adjectives and decide whether repetition is useful for cohesion or merely redundant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep deliberate repetition of key terms; revise to remove lazy or aimless repetition that repeats the same point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write your thesis in five different ways
rubrics_metrics.description: Generating multiple formulations of the thesis helps reveal choices and opportunities to improve clarity and emphasis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose five variants and choose or combine phrasings to produce a stronger, clearer thesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read your paper aloud (slowly) to check clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Reading aloud makes awkward or confusing phrasing more apparent to the writer and listeners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read alone or with a partner; if listeners understand your argument easily, ensure the written version matches that clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Talk through your argument concisely (oral outline) to test clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Explaining the argument out loud in concise form helps test whether your written words are as clear as your oral presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an outsider can quickly grasp your main point and significance verbally, revise the written paper to match that clarity; if not, work on clearer terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have someone unfamiliar with the issue read your paper
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'outsider' reader can reveal words or sentences they find confusing even if you assume confusion stems from topic knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not dismiss their confusion as lack of knowledge; rewrite so that an unfamiliar reader can follow at all times.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a self-question checklist while revising
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask targeted questions to evaluate word choice and key-term use (e.g., Do I know each word's meaning? Am I trying to impress? What are my key terms? Are they too specific or too vague?).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work through the questions to decide whether to look up words, find better terms in your vocabulary or sources, and test whether key terms cover the intended range of your argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consult related handouts/resources for style, passive voice, proofreading
rubrics_metrics.description: Word choice revision links to broader issues of style, voice, and editing that are covered in other resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to supplementary handouts on style, passive voice, and proofreading; check works consulted for further reading and periodically revisit tips.
